## Executive summary
**Bland AI has opened a direct positioning attack on orchestration-based voice platforms like Retell, arguing that owning and self-hosting the entire STT/LLM/TTS stack — not SOC 2/HIPAA certifications — is the #1 vendor selection criterion for regulated contact-center buyers.**

**1. The competitive frame is shifting from compliance badges to infrastructure ownership.** Bland's new 'Voice AI for Contact Centers: Build vs. Buy' post explicitly tells buyers to ask whether a vendor owns and hosts its speech-to-text, LLM inference, TTS and orchestration, or resells third-party models — and calls reselling 'disqualifying' for highly-regulated buyers. It claims self-hosted TTS trained in-house, own LLM inference (including post-call analysis), bare-metal hosting, a dedicated orchestration server per customer, optional dedicated GPUs with customer-controlled model promotion/rollback, VPC and on-prem deployment, and direct SIP. This is a deliberate attempt to reframe our best-of-breed orchestration and BYO-LLM flexibility as 'no control over the model layer' in exactly the healthcare, insurance and enterprise deals where we win today on HIPAA/SOC 2.

**2. Bland is also closing the product gap on our core builder and QA surface area.** The same post details Conversational Pathways (node graphs with in-node LLM conversation, loop conditions, custom code, real-time API calls, variable extraction, global prompt), plus 'Console' — a Cursor-style text interface for editing pathway nodes — node-level testing, simulated calls, regression testing, pathway logs, and post-call analysis that cites exact timestamps and source material for every extracted data point. Production features listed include warm transfers, live translation, SMS, long-term memory, appointment scheduling and latency monitoring. Two claims are genuine differentiators against us right now: AI/text-driven flow editing and citation-backed extraction with jump-to-timestamp verification — the latter is a powerful trust argument for healthcare/insurance QA buyers.

**3. A price-leadership narrative is being built on top of the infrastructure story.** Bland rates its own unit economics as 'bare metal, best-in-class unit cost' versus 'marked-up third-party AI + PS fees' for managed services, and attacks outcome-based pricing bundled with professional services. No per-minute rates were published, but the implied discovery question — 'your price includes someone else's margin' — will land squarely on our usage-based per-minute pricing in high-volume contact-center deals.

**4. Bland is simultaneously buying SMB share of voice and writing us out of the comparison set.** A 40k-character listicle, '13 Best AI Answering Services for Emerging and Growing Businesses', ranks Bland #1 and lists twelve SMB players with prices (Rosie from $49/mo unlimited, IsOn24 $49/mo for 1,000 minutes, Ringly $99/mo minimum, Sona $25/mo for 40 calls to $199/mo for 600 calls). Retell AI does not appear. Bland is defining the 'AI answering service' category for the exact segments we sell into — home services, healthcare practices, appointment scheduling — while routing that traffic to its enterprise motion.

**What we should do:** (a) ship a rebuttal battlecard within two weeks covering pinned/versioned models, BYO-LLM, model-change notification, tenancy isolation, subprocessor list, DPAs and HIPAA BAA; (b) make a roadmap decision on a dedicated/VPC or private-deployment tier for regulated accounts; (c) prioritize timestamp-cited post-call extraction and regression-test suites; (d) refresh per-minute TCO math and volume-tier discount guardrails; (e) publish a comparison page that puts Retell back into the 'AI answering service / AI receptionist' keyword cluster, including vertical variants.

**Watch list**
- Whether Bland converts its VPC/on-prem and dedicated-GPU claims into a named, priced enterprise tier or public security/architecture documentation we can compete against line-by-line.
- Any public per-minute or per-outcome pricing from Bland that substantiates its 'best-in-class unit cost' claim — this would force a response on our per-minute rate card.
- General availability and depth of 'Console' (AI/text-based pathway editing) and whether node-level plus regression testing becomes a standard RFP requirement in our deals.
- Bland's SEO expansion into vertical answering-service keywords (HVAC, dental, legal intake) and whether it starts naming Retell in comparison content.
- Whether other competitors adopt the same 'we own the whole stack' framing, turning infrastructure ownership into a category-wide buying criterion rather than a Bland-specific pitch.

## Coverage
| Competitor | Pages scanned | Changes detected | Insights |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Bland AI | 44 | 3 | 4 |

## Bland AI
### 🔴 Bland publishes a build-vs-buy guide that attacks 'reseller' voice platforms and positions self-hosted infrastructure as the #1 buying criterion
_Content / marketing · high significance_

A new long-form post, 'Voice AI for Contact Centers: Build vs. Buy', argues the most important question to ask any vendor is whether they own and host STT, LLM inference, TTS and orchestration, or resell third-party models. Bland claims it self-hosts the entire pipeline, trained its own TTS models, runs its own LLM inference (including post-call analysis), runs on bare metal, and gives each customer a dedicated orchestration server plus optionally dedicated GPUs with customer-controlled model promotion/rollback. It frames reliance on third-party providers as 'disqualifying' for highly-regulated buyers, citing risks of unannounced model updates, ToS/data-policy changes, provider breaches, price changes and multi-tenant opacity. It also advertises VPC and on-prem deployment of the full stack and direct SIP integration.

**Implications for Retell AI:** This is a direct, named-category attack on platforms like Retell AI that orchestrate best-of-breed third-party STT/LLM/TTS and offer BYO-LLM. Expect this argument in enterprise, healthcare, insurance and regulated-vertical deals where we currently win on HIPAA/SOC 2: Bland is moving the goalposts from certifications to infrastructure ownership, dedicated tenancy, model version control/rollback and VPC/on-prem. Our BYO-LLM flexibility can be reframed by Bland as 'you have no control over the model layer'.

**Recommended action:** PM + Sales: build a one-page rebuttal/battlecard within two weeks covering our model-layer controls (pinned/versioned models, BYO-LLM, model change notification, tenancy isolation, subprocessor list, DPAs, HIPAA BAA) and decide whether to productize a dedicated/VPC or private-deployment tier for regulated accounts; PM to scope feasibility and pricing.

Evidence: <https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy>

### 🔴 Bland discloses Pathways tooling detail: Console (Cursor-style pathway editor), node-level testing, regression testing, cited post-call analysis and call guardrails
_Product update · high significance_

The build-vs-buy post details Bland's developer workflow: Conversational Pathways as a graph of nodes with LLM-driven conversation inside nodes, loop conditions between nodes, custom code execution, real-time API calls, variable extraction and a global prompt that applies across all nodes. It names 'Console', described as a Cursor-style text interface for editing specific pathway nodes, plus node-level testing, simulated calls, regression testing, pathway logs, and post-call analysis that cites exact timestamps and source material for every extracted data point. It also lists production 'long tail' features: warm transfers, live translation, real-time code execution, SMS, long-term memory, appointment scheduling and latency monitoring. Self-serve free signup at app.bland.ai is promoted.

**Implications for Retell AI:** This maps almost feature-for-feature onto Retell's Conversation Flow, agent testing/simulation and post-call analysis, with two areas where Bland now claims an edge: AI/text-based flow editing (Console), node-level plus regression testing, and evidence-cited post-call extraction with jump-to-timestamp verification. Cited extraction is a strong trust feature for healthcare/insurance QA buyers and a likely objection in bake-offs.

**Recommended action:** PM: run a hands-on evaluation of Bland's free tier (Pathways, Console, node/regression testing, citations) and prioritize timestamp-cited post-call extraction and regression-test suites on our roadmap for the next quarter; Eng to scope citation-linked analysis on existing transcripts.

Evidence: <https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy>

### 🟡 Bland makes a unit-economics argument: 'bare metal, best-in-class unit cost' vs marked-up resellers and outcome-priced managed services
_Pricing change · medium significance_

In the comparison table, Bland rates its own unit economics as 'Bare metal, best-in-class unit cost', building on open source as 'Expensive at small scale', and managed services as 'Marked-up third-party AI + PS fees'. It explicitly criticizes vendors using outcomes-based pricing (per resolution/per outcome) bundled with professional services as having 'significantly higher' unit economics, while noting Bland's own Forward Deployment Engineering team is supplemental rather than a paid implementation model. No specific prices or per-minute rates are published in this material.

**Implications for Retell AI:** Bland is setting up a price-leadership narrative grounded in owning its own inference, which pressures our usage-based per-minute pricing in high-volume contact-center deals where per-minute cost is the primary line item. Sales should expect 'your price includes someone else's margin' as a discovery question in competitive cycles.

**Recommended action:** Sales + Finance: refresh the per-minute TCO comparison (including telephony, LLM, TTS pass-through and any concurrency fees) and define volume-tier discount guardrails for high-minute contact-center deals before the next quarter's renewals.

Evidence: <https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy>

### 🟡 Bland ramps SEO listicle content targeting SMB 'AI answering service' buyers, ranking itself #1 and omitting Retell entirely
_Content / marketing · medium significance_

A new 40k-character post, '13 Best AI Answering Services for Emerging and Growing Businesses', ranks Bland #1 ('best for enterprises requiring self-hosted, real-time voice agents that replace call center operations entirely') and lists Smith.ai, Goodcall, Upfirst, My AI Front Desk, Ruby, Allo, Rosie, Sona by Quo, IsOn24, Ringly, Marlie and Greetmate with prices (e.g. Rosie unlimited from $49/mo, IsOn24 $49/mo for 1,000 minutes, Ringly $99/mo minimum, Sona $25/mo for 40 calls up to $199/mo for 600 calls). The piece is heavily stat-loaded ($126k annual loss from missed calls, 62% of inbound calls unanswered, 5-minute response = 21x conversion) and repeatedly cites Bland's SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR compliance plus a 15-minute demo CTA. Retell AI does not appear in the list.

**Implications for Retell AI:** Bland is buying share of voice on mid-funnel SMB/vertical answering-service keywords while still routing traffic to its enterprise page, and it is defining the comparison set without us in it. That costs us consideration with the exact segments we sell into (home services, healthcare practices, appointment scheduling) and lets Bland own the 'AI answering service' category framing.

**Recommended action:** Marketing: publish or refresh a competing 'best AI answering service / AI receptionist' comparison page that includes Retell and Bland with accurate per-minute pricing and compliance facts, and target the same keyword cluster plus the vertical variants (HVAC, dental, legal intake) this quarter.

Evidence: <https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services> · <https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy>

## Executive summary
**Bland AI closed a $50M Series C, claims the first FedRAMP 20x certification, and launched a pricing page that names Retell by name and reframes our ~$0.07/min as a misleading partial rate.**

**1. Bland is now funded, credentialed, and attacking us directly.** A $50M Series C (Scale, Emergence, HubSpot, Dell Technologies Capital, Upfront; >$100M total) plus claims of 3.5M+ calls/week and named logos in our core ICPs (Samsara, Kin Insurance, CNO Financial, Mutual of Omaha, First Financial Bank, Medallion, Innovaccer). They also claim to be the first company in America with FedRAMP 20x certification, obtained in 18 days, and have launched a /government page targeting VA, SSA and IRS call centers. That is a public-sector TAM we cannot bid on today and a hard disqualifier lever in any regulated RFP.

**2. Pricing is now a public, named fight.** Bland's new pricing page publishes Start $0.14/min ($0 platform fee), Build $0.12/min (+$299/mo), Scale $0.11/min (+$499/mo), with transfers at $0.04–$0.05/min and telephony at carrier pass-through. It explicitly states Retell 'lists about $0.07/min' but that real stacks land at '$0.11 to $0.25 per minute on Retell.' Our BYO-LLM flexibility is being reframed as cost opacity plus a subprocessor/data-path compliance risk. We need an all-in cost calculator and a rebuttal page, not a defensive footnote.

**3. Product moves land squarely on our differentiators.** Evals (LLM-judge scoring of up to 5,000 real calls per run, 14 QA templates, pass thresholds, regression detection) overlaps our testing/simulation and post-call analysis but at production scale with compliance-audit framing. Norm generates production agents, pathways and personas from a prompt with diffs and pre-deploy simulation — a direct hit on time-to-first-agent. Bland Speech v3 (claimed #1 on Design Arena Audio Realism, 133K free characters then $0.015/1K chars, instant cloning) plus Fluent STT (5.9% WER vs 8.1% for 'the leading real-time provider') plus Noise Cancellation V2 (16% WER gain across 3,744 live calls) and adaptive resumption (manual turn-taking config removed entirely) give them owned, benchmark-backed infrastructure they bundle at no token markup.

**4. They are going omnichannel and CRM-triggered.** Branded iMessage agents with shared pathways/persona memory across voice and SMS, plus Salesforce record-change triggers that fire outbound AI calls into specific pathways. Note for Sales: iMessage, SMS/Web Chat, SMS Node and the Appointment Scheduling Node are all Enterprise-gated.

**5. Two real openings for us.** Bland published hard self-serve ceilings — 10/50/100 concurrent calls and 100/2,000/5,000 calls per day — which is below what most contact-center and outbound-heavy buyers need, forcing them into custom Enterprise. And the Enterprise-only column (guardrails, SSO, JWT signatures, data residency, dedicated orchestration, BAA, on-prem/VPC, forward-deployed engineers, 28–30 day deployment framework) is a checklist prospects will hand us; every gap there is a disqualifier, every parity item is a margin argument against their $299–$499/mo platform fees.

**6. Content is an industrial operation, not a campaign.** '13 Best Bland.ai Alternatives' ranks Retell #2 then undercuts us ('inference still routes through third-party providers, so compliance coverage applies to the application layer, not the full data path'). Category hubs, a /blog/library archive back to 2024, 60+ pages of pagination, and TCO/buyer-framework assets mean they are writing the evaluation criteria before buyers reach us.

**Watch list**
- Whether Bland's FedRAMP 20x claim converts into named federal agency wins or a Marketplace-verified listing — and whether the certification language starts appearing in commercial regulated RFPs (healthcare, insurance, banking) as a disqualifier for us.
- Bland Scale tier confirmation and any pricing movement: does $0.11/min get undercut further, do platform fees change, or do Enterprise-gated features (SMS, iMessage, Appointment Scheduling Node) move down-tier to attack our mid-market.

### 🔴 Bland launches Evals: LLM-judge scoring of up to 5,000 real calls per run with 14 prebuilt QA templates

Named wins in insurance, financial services and healthcare overlap directly with Retell's core ICPs, so we should expect them in more of our competitive deals with heavier implementation support.
insights.recommended_action: Sales + Exec: run a win/loss review on deals where Bland was shortlisted in insurance, healthcare and financial services, and define our counter-offer to their forward-deployed-engineer model (e.g. packaged implementation or partner-led deployment SKU).

insights.title: Bland ships Bland Speech v3 as a standalone TTS product with free tier and $0.015/1K-character pricing
insights.summary: Bland launched 'Bland Speech,' a developer TTS platform whose first model, Speech v3, is claimed #1 on Design Arena's Audio Realism Benchmark (Elo 1365) ahead of ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Cartesia and xAI, beaten only by human recordings. It was trained on 5M+ hours of audio and 100M+ real human conversations, exposes POST /v1/speak returning PCM16 WAV at 44.1 kHz with HTTP-chunked and WebSocket streaming, and includes a studio ('Director'), performance tags like [laughs], instant cloning from ~10 seconds of audio and professional cloning from 30+ minutes. New accounts get 133,000 free characters (~2 hours), then $0.015 per 1,000 characters; a $5 credit load unlocks professional cloning. Plans include 1/5/15 voice clones on Start/Build/Scale.
insights.implications_for_us: Bland now owns a benchmark-backed voice model it can bundle into its per-minute rate at no token markup, which weakens our 'choose best-in-class voices' advantage on both quality and cost. It also gives them a top-of-funnel developer product that recruits builders before they ever compare agent platforms.
insights.recommended_action: PM: benchmark Retell's default and premium voice options against Bland Speech v3 on latency and blind-preference tests, and decide whether to negotiate bundled TTS pricing or ship a first-party low-cost voice tier.

insights.title: Bland launches Evals: LLM-judge scoring of up to 5,000 real calls per run with 14 prebuilt QA templates
insights.summary: Bland Evals grades real or test calls using LLM judges that read transcripts and listen to audio, scoring dimensions like resolution, tone, hallucination, prompt/pathway adherence, objection handling, audio quality, appointment-booked and transfer-request behavior. Users create a Workbench, select up to 5,000 calls, attach up to 10 eval agents (from 14 templates or custom), set a pass threshold, and get per-call verdicts plus aggregate score distributions; 'insufficient evidence' verdicts are excluded from averages. Norm can auto-generate eval agents from a described customer issue, and evals are positioned for regression detection across prompt/pathway changes and for QA/compliance auditing at scale.
insights.implications_for_us: This directly overlaps Retell's agent testing/simulation and post-call analysis, but at production scale and with explicit compliance-audit framing. Buyers in contact centers and regulated verticals will ask whether Retell can score thousands of live calls automatically, not just run pre-launch simulations.
insights.recommended_action: PM: assess gap between Retell's post-call analysis/testing and batch LLM-judge scoring at 1,000+ call scale, and prioritize a bulk call-quality scoring feature with prebuilt rubrics on the next roadmap cycle.

insights.title: Bland adds branded iMessage agents plus Salesforce event-triggered outbound calls, pushing beyond voice-only
insights.summary: Bland launched iMessage support that shares pathways, personas and persona memory with voice and SMS agents; enterprise plans get a verified branded business profile, blue bubbles, high-res media and document exchange, tapbacks, voice memos, delivery/read receipts, typing indicators and encryption. Separately, new event-based automations trigger AI calls when a Salesforce record changes, using Events (lead/opportunity/case created or updated), Conditions on custom Salesforce fields, and Actions (AI call, Slack notification, webhook), with routing into different pathways for second touches, reschedules and case follow-ups. The pricing table gates SMS & Web Chat, Appointment Scheduling Node, SMS Node and iMessage to Enterprise only.
insights.implications_for_us: Bland is converting from an AI-phone vendor into an omnichannel agent platform with unified memory, which strengthens its enterprise story against a voice-first competitor. CRM-event-triggered calling also encroaches on the lead-qualification and appointment-reminder workflows Retell sells, where trigger reliability is a common buyer question.
insights.recommended_action: PM: validate Retell's CRM-event trigger coverage (Salesforce/HubSpot record-change to outbound call) and decide whether unified voice+SMS memory belongs on the roadmap; Sales should note iMessage is Enterprise-gated when countering omnichannel claims.

insights.title: Bland removes manual turn-taking config with adaptive resumption and ships Noise Cancellation V2 (16% WER gain)
insights.summary: An August 3, 2026 changelog entry introduces 'adaptive resumption': agents measure each caller's speech length and mid-thought pause duration and adjust response timing automatically, matching a pace change within ~15 seconds; the resumption_speed field is removed entirely so there is no manual timing setting. The same release scopes per-node interruptibility settings and interruption thresholds to the active node only, reverting to the agent default on exit. Separately, Noise Cancellation V2 was measured across 3,744 live production calls and improves Word Error Rate by 16%, filtering audio upstream of the transcriber; it can be enabled per Persona, per Send Call, or per inbound number.
insights.implications_for_us: Turn-taking tuning and barge-in thresholds are recurring sources of customer complaints and support load for voice agent platforms, and Bland is turning them into zero-config defaults with measured evidence. Expect prospects to ask how Retell handles interruption thresholds, slow callers and noisy environments without manual tuning.
insights.recommended_action: Eng + PM: run a comparative test of Retell's interruption/endpointing defaults against slow, fast and noisy caller profiles, and evaluate shipping adaptive endpointing plus an upstream noise-suppression toggle with published WER deltas.

insights.title: Norm AI assistant lets users build and edit voice agents from a prompt, including over iMessage
insights.summary: Bland positions Norm as 'the first AI assistant that builds production-ready voice agents from a prompt,' generating prompts, personas, agents and pathways from natural language, with diff comparison between old and new prompts, safe branching before deploy, mid-conversation API calls with request testing, agent-on-agent simulations, and file/knowledge-base attachment. Bland frames Norm as codifying the knowledge of its forward-deployed engineers so 'every customer' gets the equivalent. A public Norm iMessage agent at +1 (321) 424-0172 can create/update agents, run simulations, pull analytics, generate PDF/Excel reports and schedule recurring digests.
insights.implications_for_us: Norm attacks time-to-first-agent, the metric that most often decides self-serve trials, and it also reduces Bland's own services burden. If prospects can describe a flow and get a working pathway in minutes, Retell's Conversation Flow builder needs a comparable natural-language generation and safe-diff/deploy workflow.
insights.recommended_action: PM: prototype prompt-to-pathway generation with versioned diffs and simulation-before-deploy in Retell's Conversation Flow builder, and instrument time-to-first-successful-test-call as the tracked metric.

insights.title: Bland publishes hard plan limits (10/50/100 concurrency, daily caps, knowledge bases) and a 99.9% uptime SLA on all tiers
insights.summary: The pricing comparison table now exposes concrete ceilings: Start allows 10 concurrent calls, 100 calls/day, 100 calls/hour, 1 voice and 10 knowledge bases; Build allows 50 concurrent, 2,000/day, 1,000/hour, 5 voices and 50 knowledge bases; Scale (referenced in blog posts at $499/mo) allows 100 concurrent, 5,000/day and 100 knowledge bases; Enterprise is unlimited with concurrency sized to volume. A 99.9% uptime SLA is listed on all three tiers, while dedicated orchestration server, priority call queue, on-prem/VPC, custom voice actor, warm and live transfers, guardrails, alarm & monitoring, knowledge base gaps, citations, outcomes, custom dialing, custom code extraction, BAA, SSO, JWT signatures, data residency, Slack channel and forward-deployed engineers are Enterprise-only.
insights.implications_for_us: The published caps are a sales opening: Bland's self-serve tiers top out at 100 concurrent calls and 5,000 calls/day, which is below what many contact-center and outbound-heavy buyers need, forcing them into a custom Enterprise contract. At the same time the Enterprise column is a checklist prospects will hand us, so any gaps in our own guardrails, SSO, JWT signing or data residency become disqualifiers.
insights.recommended_action: Sales: build a limits-comparison battlecard contrasting Retell concurrency and batch-calling headroom against Bland's 10/50/100 tiers, and have PM confirm parity on the Enterprise checklist items (guardrails, SSO, JWT, data residency, dedicated orchestration).

insights.title: Bland standardizes on a 28–30 day forward-deployed-engineer deployment framework with on-prem/VPC and BAA
insights.summary: Across the pricing page, homepage and multiple posts, Bland promotes a structured enterprise rollout: 'Enterprise deployments, live in production in 30 days' with milestones at Day 01 discovery, Day 07 build, Day 14 first end-to-end run with cloned voice, Day 21 dry run and safety locks, Day 30 live. The pricing page describes a '28-day deployment framework: scope, build, gray/red/green-team test, and go live' staffed by forward-deployed engineers, alongside on-prem/VPC deployment, BAA, SSO, data residency, encryption (AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3, HSM-backed keys), 24/7 on-call and SLA-bound incident notifications. Homepage also claims 40+ languages with real-time translation in 23 and mid-call language switching.
insights.implications_for_us: Bland is competing on assisted time-to-value, not just product, which is persuasive to regulated buyers who fear a self-serve build. If Retell sells primarily as a self-serve/dev-first platform, we risk losing enterprise deals on perceived implementation risk even when our product matches.
insights.recommended_action: Sales + PM: package a named Retell enterprise onboarding program with a committed go-live window, security-review artifacts and testing stages, and publish our language coverage and mid-call language-switch capability to counter the 40+/23 claim.

insights.title: Fluent multilingual STT claims 5.9% WER, beating a 'leading real-time voice AI provider' at 8.1%
insights.summary: Bland released Fluent, a multilingual speech-to-text model for real-time two-way calls, reporting ~5.9% WER in English across 250+ hours of real-world audio versus ~8.1% for 'the leading real-time voice AI transcription provider' and ~6.5% for Whisper. Fluent covers six languages (English, Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Italian) with automatic language detection and native intra-utterance code-switching, and Bland highlights improved VAD/end-of-speech detection that reduces interjections and lowers effective latency. It is selectable via language: 'fluent' and falls back automatically to Bland's Auto model (10 languages); Babel remains for ~99 languages.
insights.implications_for_us: Transcription accuracy and endpointing quality directly drive containment and CSAT in healthcare and insurance calls, and Bland now has a published WER number to wave in bake-offs. Their three-tier STT strategy (Fluent for precision, Auto for range, Babel for reach) also gives them a clean answer to multilingual requirements.
insights.recommended_action: Eng: run a head-to-head WER and endpointing benchmark of Retell's STT options against Fluent on noisy, accented and code-switched call audio, and publish results if favorable.

insights.title: Bland reorganizes its blog into taxonomy hubs and an archive, signaling a durable SEO structure
insights.summary: Alongside the new posts, Bland has stood up category hubs for Industry deep-dives, Product & company news, Voice AI guides, Conversational AI, Contact-center automation and Comparisons & alternatives, plus a full '/blog/library' archive listing dated posts back through early 2024 and paginated indexes reaching at least page 60. Industry hubs cluster around healthcare, insurance, hotels, restaurants and telecom, and the library surfaces buyer-intent assets like 'Total cost of ownership: AI voice agents vs call center staff', 'Voice AI pricing: what enterprises actually pay in 2026' and 'How to evaluate AI voice agent platforms in 2026: a buyer's framework'.
insights.implications_for_us: This is infrastructure for sustained organic capture across exactly the verticals Retell sells into, including TCO and buyer-framework content that shapes evaluation criteria before vendor contact. It suggests a funded content operation rather than a one-off campaign.
insights.recommended_action: Marketing: audit our vertical content coverage against Bland's category hubs (healthcare, insurance, home services, contact center) and prioritize a Retell TCO and evaluation-framework asset to compete for the same buyer-stage queries.

# 13 Best AI Answering Services for Emerging and Growing Businesses
Your phone rings at 2 AM. Then again at lunch. Then three more times while you're in a client meeting. Growing businesses face a persistent challenge: every missed call could be a lost customer, but hiring enough staff to answer every inquiry around the clock isn't financially sustainable.
Modern AI answering services solve this problem by acting like skilled receptionists who never take breaks. Instead of letting calls go to voicemail or forcing customers to navigate clunky phone trees, these systems engage callers naturally, answer common questions, schedule appointments, and route complex issues to the right person. The result is faster response times and consistent customer experiences that scale with your business, not your payroll. [Bland's conversational AI](https://www.bland.ai/enterprise) delivers exactly this type of seamless overflow call handling for businesses ready to transform their customer service approach.
## Summary[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#summary)
* Missed calls cost small businesses an average of $126,000 annually, with 62% of inbound phone calls going unanswered according to recent industry data. The financial damage stays invisible because most companies never track the revenue that walks away when prospects hit voicemail and immediately call the next competitor. For local service businesses, a single unanswered emergency call can mean losing a $500 repair job, while professional services firms sacrifice tens of thousands in lifetime client value every time a consultation request goes to voicemail.
* Response speed determines conversion more than pricing or service quality in high-intent scenarios. Harvard Business Review research shows that leads are 21 times more likely to convert when contacted within 5 minutes than when contacted after 30 minutes. InsideSales reports that 78% of customers buy from the company that responds first, not the one with the best offer. When a homeowner calls about a burst pipe or a prospect needs urgent legal advice, the conversation happens with whoever picks up the phone, making availability the single strongest competitive advantage.
* Staffing gaps during lunch breaks, sick days, and after-hours periods create inconsistent coverage that damages customer experience even when teams are technically available. The receptionist who handles calls flawlessly at 10 AM becomes overwhelmed by 3 PM, and prospects calling during that window get rushed service or voicemail. Traditional solutions like hiring more staff or extending hours fail when call patterns shift unpredictably, leaving businesses choosing between expensive overstaffing or accepting that some high-value leads will simply vanish during coverage gaps.
* AI chatbots can handle up to 80% of routine customer queries according to IBM research, but the remaining 20% requiring human judgment to determine whether automated systems feel helpful or bureaucratic. The best platforms identify priority callers and transfer them instantly to the right person rather than forcing everyone through rigid phone trees. Intelligent escalation logic means that an "urgent account freeze" mention triggers an immediate human connection, while appointment requests and basic FAQs are resolved without consuming staff time.
* Enterprise-grade AI answering platforms now deliver response accuracy rivaling trained human agents when properly configured, according to a NextPhone study analyzing 130,175 calls. The technology maintains consistent quality across phone, SMS, and web chat without requiring separate tools for each channel. Self-hosted infrastructure options let compliance-focused businesses keep data under their control while handling complex, multi-turn conversations in real time rather than routing to scripted decision trees.
* [Bland's conversational AI](https://www.bland.ai/) addresses this by handling customer phone interactions across all channels with automated routing and real-time escalation, compressing response cycles from hours to minutes while maintaining full compliance audit trails across SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR requirements.
## Why Businesses Lose Leads From Missed Calls and Slow Response Times[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#why-businesses-lose-leads-from-missed-calls-and-slow-response-times)
For many businesses, the **biggest source of lost revenue** isn't _bad_ marketing—it's [**missed calls**](https://www.bland.ai/blog/a-complete-guide-to-ai-phone-agents-in-2024) and **delayed responses**. When a prospect calls with an **urgent problem**, that moment represents **peak [buying intent](https://www.spate.nyc/blog/understanding-consumer-intent-search-queries)**. If no one answers, they **call the next company** on the list.
![Phone ringing connected to dollar sign showing missed revenue from calls](https://www.bland.ai/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Ftmmoa80b%2Fproduction%2F2fca70cc4e6e465df457b99357650e6f82383a6a-1024x1024.webp%3Fw%3D1920&w=3840&q=75)
"Companies that respond to leads within **5 minutes** are **100 times more likely** to connect with prospects than those who wait **30 minutes** or longer." — Harvard Business Review
![Split scene comparing business answering calls versus missing calls](https://www.bland.ai/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Ftmmoa80b%2Fproduction%2Fd3c92a77efe4d806e4dc989fcb0c8051f012e8eb-1024x1024.webp%3Fw%3D1920&w=3840&q=75)
### What is the financial impact of missed calls?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#what-is-the-financial-impact-of-missed-calls)
The financial impact is substantial. Small businesses lose an average of $126,000 annually because [62% of inbound phone calls](https://pcnanswers.com/missed-call-revenue-study/) go unanswered. For a local HVAC company, a missed call means losing a $500 emergency repair to a competitor. For financial advisors or law firms, a single missed consultation can cost tens of thousands in [lifetime client value](https://executiveeducation.wharton.upenn.edu/thought-leadership/wharton-online-insights/why-customer-lifetime-value-matters/).
### How does response speed impact lead conversion rates?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#how-does-response-speed-impact-lead-conversion-rates)
Response time is the strongest predictor of [lead conversion](https://dealhub.io/glossary/lead-conversion/). [Research from Harvard Business Review](https://voiso.com/articles/lead-response-time-metrics/) shows that leads are 21 times more likely to convert when contacted within 5 minutes versus 30 minutes or longer. High-intent prospects actively compare options in real time; answering immediately often means you're their only conversation before they decide.
#### Why do customers choose the first company to respond?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#why-do-customers-choose-the-first-company-to-respond)
[InsideSales reports](https://voiso.com/articles/lead-response-time-metrics/) that 78% of customers buy from the company that responds first. A homeowner with a burst pipe needs someone immediately, not callbacks hours later. The competitor who answers on the second ring doesn't need better pricing or a stronger pitch—they simply needed to be there when it mattered.
### Why do staffing solutions create coverage gaps?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#why-do-staffing-solutions-create-coverage-gaps)
Most businesses assume that hiring more staff or installing voicemail is sufficient to handle increased phone calls. Staffing gaps occur during lunch breaks, sick days, and vacation time. After-hours calls pile up overnight and go unanswered by morning.
[Manual workflows](https://www.bland.ai/blog/5-ways-ai-call-center-agents-can-streamline-your-operations) slow down as teams grow, creating uneven coverage. A receptionist handling calls smoothly at 10 AM may be overwhelmed by 3 PM, leaving callers with a degraded experience.
#### How does conversational AI solve coverage problems?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#how-does-conversational-ai-solve-coverage-problems)
Solutions like [Bland's conversational AI](https://www.bland.ai/enterprise) handle customer phone calls, text messages, and web chat without requiring human scheduling. Large teams managing high call volumes benefit from AI that maintains consistent response quality 24/7 and [captures leads](https://www.bland.ai/solutions/lead-qualification) that would otherwise be lost during off-hours.
The technology doesn't replace human judgment for complicated issues; it ensures that no serious customer misses out on help because they called at the wrong time. But knowing missed calls cost money and understanding how to [fix the problem](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-customer-service) are two different challenges.
## How AI Answering Services Improve Customer Service and How to Choose[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#how-ai-answering-services-improve-customer-service-and-how-to-choose)
The **best AI answering services** reduce **response delays**, [qualify leads](https://www.highspot.com/blog/lead-qualification/) _instantly_, [route conversations intelligently](https://www.bland.ai/blog/advanced-call-routing), and provide **_24/7 consistency_**. This frees **human staff** to focus on _relationship-building_ that requires **judgment** and **empathy** while protecting **revenue**.
![Four icons representing AI answering service benefits: response time, instant qualification, intelligent routing, and 24/7 consistency](https://www.bland.ai/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Ftmmoa80b%2Fproduction%2F1201bfdab3c6a025761fda1f8acf628dc32e27c1-1024x1024.webp%3Fw%3D1920&w=3840&q=75)
**AI answering platforms** vary _significantly_ in **response quality**, **integrations**, [escalation handling](https://www.custify.com/blog/customer-escalations/), and **customization**. [According to Salesforce](https://www.salesforce.com/service/ai/customer-service-ai/), **_83% of customers_** expect **immediate interaction** when contacting a company. The gap between **customer urgency** and **team availability** is where **revenue leaks** occur.
"**_83% of customers_** expect **immediate interaction** when contacting a company." — Salesforce
### Response Accuracy and Natural Language Processing[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#response-accuracy-and-natural-language-processing)
The system must enable smooth, natural conversations without awkward robotic delays. A high-quality [voice agent](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents---most-common-questions-from-executives) understands when callers interrupt and naturally shifts direction. Poor [NLP](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/natural-language-processing) frustrates callers, driving them to hang up and contact your competitors instead.
### Native Appointment Scheduling and CRM Integration[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#native-appointment-scheduling-and-crm-integration)
The tool must work like a real booking system, not simply take messages. The AI should safely read your live calendar and book the consultation before the person hangs up. To eliminate manual data entry, the system must connect directly to your existing [tech stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solution_stack), sending the caller's phone number and request straight into HubSpot or Salesforce without requiring someone to copy information from voicemail.
### How does intelligent routing identify priority callers?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#how-does-intelligent-routing-identify-priority-callers)
The platform must identify priority callers and route them appropriately. If a caller mentions an "urgent account freeze," the AI should immediately escalate the request to a live support manager.
[IBM reports](https://masterofcode.com/blog/ai-in-customer-service-statistics) that AI chatbots handle [up to 80% of routine queries](https://www.chatbot.com/blog/chatbot-statistics/), but the remaining 20% requires human judgment. Handoff quality determines whether your system feels helpful or bureaucratic.
#### What makes enterprise-grade escalation systems effective?[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#what-makes-enterprise-grade-escalation-systems-effective)
[Platforms like Bland](https://www.bland.ai/enterprise) combine customer interactions with automated routing and real-time escalation, reducing response times from hours to minutes while maintaining compliance records for SOC 2 Type II, [HIPAA](https://www.bland.ai/trust-security#hipaa), and GDPR.
Enterprise-grade systems maintain consistent response quality across phone, SMS, and web chat without requiring separate tools for each channel.
### When AI Works Best (and When It Doesn't)[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#when-ai-works-best-and-when-it-doesnt)
AI answering services work especially well for [appointment-based businesses](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-appointment-scheduling), after-hours questions, and repeated customer questions. Complex legal consultations, medical diagnoses, or emotionally sensitive conversations may still require human intervention. [Hybrid models](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/next-hybrid-intelligence-systems-amplify-augment-human-capabilities) work best when AI handles overflow calls and initial screening while humans focus on building key relationships.
Choosing the right platform requires evaluating [enterprise readiness](https://www.bland.ai/blog/2024-guide-enterprise-ai-phone-agents), compliance depth, and multi-channel capabilities that serious businesses need.
## 13 Best AI Answering Services for Emerging and Growing Businesses[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#13-best-ai-answering-services-for-emerging-and-growing-businesses)
The **right AI answering service** depends on your situation: **deep platform connection**, **support for multiple languages**, **hybrid human handoff**, or **workflows for specific industries**. **Budget-conscious startups** face different challenges than **healthcare practices** needing **compliance** or **high-volume online stores**. What matters isn't the feature count, but **which one solves** your _specific_ problem, costing you **leads**, **time**, or **customer trust**.
![Split scene showing different business types with contrasting needs](https://www.bland.ai/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Ftmmoa80b%2Fproduction%2F3a10316af4059f50a7e4b7514090257c14f69594-1024x1024.webp%3Fw%3D1920&w=3840&q=75)
"**Budget-conscious startups** face _different_ challenges than **healthcare practices** that need to follow **compliance rules** - the tool that works for one won't work for the other."
![Three icons showing missed calls, scheduling, and data integration challenges](https://www.bland.ai/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Ftmmoa80b%2Fproduction%2Fa6e5c5d44b6c05897192e8a8ef6a178b51246831-1024x1024.webp%3Fw%3D1920&w=3840&q=75)
### 1\. Bland AI: Best for enterprises requiring self-hosted, real-time voice agents that replace call center operations entirely.[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/best-ai-answering-services#1-bland-ai-best-for-enterprises-requiring-self-hosted-real-time-voice-agents-that-replace-call-center-operations-entirely)
[Bland](https://www.bland.ai/enterprise) provides self-hosted conversational AI that sounds human and responds instantly while maintaining data control. [According to NextPhone's 130,175-call study](https://www.getnextphone.com/blog/best-ai-answering-services), enterprise-grade systems deliver response accuracy that matches that of trained human agents when properly configured. Large businesses use Bland for faster, more [reliable customer conversations](https://www.bland.ai/solutions/customer-service) with compliance and scalability that traditional call centers cannot match.

# Voice AI for Contact Centers: Build vs. Buy
We’ve helped hundreds of customers implement voice AI, many who came to us after trying to build it themselves or deploying other solutions. This guide breaks down what a real-world voice AI implementation actually entails, the tradeoffs between building in-house, buying a managed service, or using a developer-first platform, and where the hidden complexity tends to surface.
**What this doc covers:**
* The voice AI landscape and why infrastructure ownership is the single most important differentiator
* What a voice AI stack actually requires beyond the model layer
* Building on open source
* Using a managed service
* Using a developer platform
* An honest side-by-side comparison
## **The Voice AI Landscape**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#the-voice-ai-landscape)
The most important question to ask any voice AI vendor is: do you actually own and host the voice AI infrastructure, or are you reselling someone else's?
This is the fundamental dividing line in the market right now, and it matters far more than most buyers realize.
**What a self-hosted stack actually means.** A voice AI call has three model layers: transcription (speech-to-text), inference (the language model), and TTS (text-to-speech). On top of that sits an orchestration server that manages the conversation flow, handles telephony, and coordinates everything in real time. A vendor that self-hosts all of this owns the full pipeline. When a customer buys from that vendor, they can get their own dedicated orchestration server and dedicated GPUs for the model infrastructure. The customer literally owns their own voice AI. When they want to promote changes, roll back a model version, or test updates against a subset of call volume, they have direct control over that.
**What a reseller looks like.** Most voice AI vendors today don't own the model infrastructure. They provide an orchestration layer on top of third-party model providers. They're resellers. When you buy from them, your calls are running through someone else's transcription, someone else's language model, and someone else's TTS. You don't have a direct relationship with those providers, and you have no control over them.
**Why this matters, concretely.** When you're building on top of third-party model infrastructure you don't control:
* The provider can push model updates whenever they want. If a model change degrades your agent's behavior mid-production, you can't roll it back. You're just dealing with it.
* The provider's terms of service can change. Their data handling policies can change. Their moderation policies can change. You have no say in any of that, and your vendor doesn't either.
* If the provider has a data breach, your data was in that pipeline.
* If the provider changes pricing, your vendor's cost structure changes, and so does yours.
* You can't get dedicated infrastructure. You're on a shared, multi-tenant stack that you have zero visibility into.
For highly-regulated companies, this should be disqualifying. They should optimize for self-hosted voice AI where the full infrastructure stack is owned and operated by the vendor you have a direct contract with, where you get dedicated infrastructure, and where model changes happen on your terms.
Bland self-hosts the entire pipeline: transcription, inference, TTS, and orchestration. We trained our own TTS models. We run on bare metal. When a customer buys Bland, they get their own dedicated orchestration server, and we can provision dedicated GPUs for their model infrastructure. They control when changes get promoted. No third-party dependencies, no surprise model updates, no terms-of-service risk from providers they've never talked to.
With that context, here are the three paths.
## **What a Voice AI Stack Actually Requires**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#what-a-voice-ai-stack-actually-requires)
The core pipeline is straightforward: speech-to-text, language model inference, and text-to-speech. You already know what those are.
What's less obvious is everything around that pipeline that a production contact center deployment actually needs: telephony integration (SIP trunking into existing phone systems), call routing and transfer logic, post-call analytics, observability and monitoring, regression testing and QA tooling, guardrails you can define on top of calls, compliance and data handling controls, and an interface for non-engineers to manage and iterate on agent behavior.
The model layer gets all the attention, but the surrounding infrastructure is where most of the ongoing work lives.
## **Building on Open Source**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#building-on-open-source)
Using an open-source framework like LiveKit, your team assembles the stack from components. LiveKit handles the real-time audio transport layer and provides some baseline tooling for connecting models to voice streams. You bring your own models and build everything above the transport layer.
**Where this makes sense:**
If your team is building a _product_, a novel, vertical voice AI solution that doesn't exist yet, building from components gives you maximum control. If you have a team of voice AI engineers who want to own and evolve a deeply custom system, open source is the right call.
**Where it gets hard:**
Self-hosting transcription, inference, and TTS models means your team needs to:
* Procure and manage GPU infrastructure, including autoscaling policies (peak hours vs. off-hours), hardware procurement cycles, and capacity planning. At smaller call volumes, the unit economics of dedicated GPUs are punishing.
* Become experts in model serving. Configuring model inference for low-latency voice, where every 100ms matters, is a specific discipline. It's not the same as deploying a chatbot.
* Solve TTS quality. Open-source TTS has improved, but it's still noticeably behind the best proprietary options. Bland had to train its own TTS models to get quality to an acceptable level for production contact centers. If you're building, you're either accepting lower quality or investing heavily here.
* Build the platform layer from scratch. LiveKit gives you audio transport. It does not give you regression testing, post-call analytics, simulation tooling, warm transfer logic, or any of the other operational infrastructure a contact center needs.
* Develop voice AI prompting expertise. Prompting a voice agent is meaningfully different from prompting a text-based LLM. The output has to be functionally correct _and_ sound natural when spoken aloud.
* Maintain it indefinitely. The build isn't a one-time cost. Models need to be updated, infrastructure needs to be patched, and the system needs continuous improvement as call patterns change.
Overall, building makes sense if you're creating a new voice AI product. If you're modernizing a contact center, you're taking on the ongoing cost and complexity of maintaining a voice AI platform as a side project to your actual mission.
## **Using Managed Services**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#using-managed-services)
Many vendors operate on outcomes-based pricing and lean heavily on their own professional services teams to build out your implementation. You're not getting a self-serve platform. You're getting a team that builds for you, and you pay per resolution or per outcome.
**Where this makes sense:**
If you're a large enterprise that wants to hand off the entire problem, doesn't need deep technical control, and is comfortable with a vendor's team owning the implementation, this model can work.
**Where it breaks down:**
**They don't own the stack.** They are wrapping third-party voice models. They're resellers. All of the risks outlined in the landscape section apply here directly: no control over model updates, no ability to roll back, no dedicated infrastructure, and exposure to third-party terms of service and data handling changes.
**They're chat-first businesses.** Their platforms were architected for chat, and voice is a newer addition. This matters because voice is a harder problem than chat. Latency requirements are tighter, conversational dynamics are more complex, and the quality bar is higher. A platform designed for chat and extended to voice will have different architectural tradeoffs than one built for voice from day one.
**Limited developer control.** They operate more like a single-prompt agent. You can't design complex, multi-stage conversations, and they don't offer API endpoints for core operations like dispatching outbound calls or pulling call data into your own systems of record. Some may have more of a graph-based interface, but none are built for technical teams that wants to iterate directly on the implementation.
**Cost structure.** Because these vendors are marking up third-party AI providers _and_ bundling in professional services, the unit economics are significantly higher.
‍
## **Using a Developer Platform**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#using-a-developer-platform)
Bland is a voice-first, developer-first platform. You can [sign up](https://app.bland.ai/) and start building for free. Your team owns the implementation directly, with support from our deployment engineers when you want it.
We offer the platform layer for building and designing conversational agents, full observability into every call, guardrails you can define on top of calls, extensive APIs for both inbound and outbound, and your own dedicated voice AI infrastructure. Here's what that looks like in practice.
**Dedicated infrastructure per customer.** Each customer gets their own dedicated orchestration server, and we can provision dedicated GPUs for model infrastructure. You control when changes get promoted. You can spin up separate containers for testing new versions of the stack, routing a portion of call volume to staging before promoting to production. Model updates happen on your terms.
**Fully self-hosted stack.** Transcription, inference, TTS, orchestration: all owned and hosted by Bland. We trained our own TTS models. We run our own LLM inference, including for post-call analysis. No third-party dependencies. We run on bare metal and control our own unit economics, which translates to competitive pricing.
**VPC and on-prem deployment.** We support deploying the full stack within your network boundary.
**SIP integration.** We connect directly into existing telephony infrastructure via SIP. Your team keeps its own phone systems and telephony rails.
**Robust APIs.** Everything in the platform can be controlled programmatically. Dispatch outbound calls, pull call data into your own systems of record, manage agents, configure pathways: all available via API.
**Conversational Pathways.** This is how you build agents on Bland. Pathways let you design conversations as a graph of nodes, where each node represents a phase of the conversation. Within a node, the LLM drives fluid, open-ended conversation. Between nodes, loop conditions define the conditional logic for when the agent moves from one stage to the next. You can execute custom code, make real-time API requests to interact with systems of record, and extract variables throughout the flow. There's also a global prompt that applies across all nodes, so you get holistic behavioral instructions alongside node-specific depth without blowing up your context window.
**Observability and Citations.** Every interaction is fully observable. You can see which nodes were hit, what decisions the agent made, and why. Post-call analysis cites exact timestamps and source material, so a human can go back and listen to the specific moment in the call to verify any extracted data point.
**Guardrails.** You can define guardrails on top of calls to ensure agents stay within policy boundaries, handle sensitive topics appropriately, and escalate when needed.
**The long tail of production.** This is where we differentiate. Getting a voice AI demo working is relatively easy. Getting it into production, and keeping it there reliably, requires handling a long tail of things: warm transfers, live translation, real-time code execution, SMS, long-term memory, appointment scheduling, latency monitoring, and more. We've built for that long tail because it's what our largest customers actually need.
**Forward Deployment Engineering (FDE) team.** Our deployment team specializes in voice AI agent design and prompting. They support implementation from day one, but this is supplemental to your team's work, not a replacement for it. You own the implementation.
## **Speed of Iteration: How You Actually Build on Bland**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#speed-of-iteration-how-you-actually-build-on-bland)
Speed of build-out and iteration is often the deciding factor for technical teams that move quickly, so it's worth describing the actual workflow.
You design your conversation in Pathways, with each phase of the call getting its own node, prompts, and logic. You test individual nodes in isolation using node-level testing. You run simulated calls to validate end-to-end behavior. You deploy, and then you use pathway logs and citations to understand exactly what's happening in production. When you need to make changes, Console (our Cursor-style text interface for pathways) lets you iterate on specific nodes without navigating through the entire graph manually. And regression testing ensures your changes don't break other parts of the agent.
Your team moves at its own pace. You're not waiting on a vendor's professional services team to make changes. You're not debugging a black box. You have full observability, direct control, and the testing infrastructure to iterate confidently.
‍
## **Comparison**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#comparison)
| Build | Managed Service | Developer Platform
Infrastructure ownership | You own it, you manage it | Third-party (resold) | Self-hosted by Bland, dedicated per customer
Model control | Full | None, provider pushes updates | Full, dedicated GPUs, rollback capability
Time to production | Months | Weeks, but vendor-dependent | Weeks, your team drives
Who owns the implementation | Your team | Vendor's PS team | Your team, with FDE support
Speed of iteration | Limited by internal capacity | Limited by vendor's team | Direct, fast, self-serve
Voice vs. chat focus | Depends on what you build | Chat-first | Voice-first
Conversation depth | Whatever you build | Single-prompt or basic graph | Pathways: node-level, LLM + deterministic
Observability | Build from scratch | Varies | Full pathway logs, cited post-call analysis
Regression testing | Build from scratch | Limited | Node-level testing, regression testing
APIs | N/A (you own the code) | Limited or none | Full API control, inbound and outbound
Deployment flexibility | Full control | Cloud only | VPC or on-prem, dedicated infra
Unit economics | Expensive at small scale | Marked-up third-party AI + PS fees | Bare metal, best-in-class unit cost
Best for | Building a voice AI product | Outsourcing the problem | VTechnical teams that want to move fast
‍
## **Conclusion**[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/voice-ai-for-contact-centers-build-vs-buy#conclusion)
If you're building a voice AI product as a core competency, open-source frameworks give you full control, but are expensive and slow.
If you want to fully outsource the problem, a managed service can work, but you're giving up control, paying a premium, depending on someone else's team to move at your pace, and building on top of third-party model infrastructure you have no relationship with and no control over.
If the goal is to move fast, own the implementation, and have a self-hosted, dedicated voice AI stack under the hood, a developer-first voice platform is the right category. Bland is worth evaluating because we own the full infrastructure stack top to bottom, we're voice-first, we support the deployment models highly-regulated companies need, and we've built for the long tail of things that actually matter in production.
If you’re interested in learning more about how we work with highly-regulated companies, you can book a meeting with us [here](https://www.bland.ai/enterprise).

# AI Phone Agents: Revolutionizing Call Center Technology and Profitability
## I. Introduction[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#i-introduction)
‍
The call center business model has always been linear in scale. More call volume means more staff and the headaches that come with managing large teams. Within Increased competition and connectivity allowing many offshore facilities deliver adequate service many operators are forced to increase their volumes.
‍
Like any business dependent on people to grow, profitability is often directly correlated to the ability to recruit, train and retain call operators; something that is notoriously difficult to do.
‍
AI phone agents are the key to unlocking exponential growth and returns for call center owners and operators. The technology has finally arrived making it feasible to scale call volumes without needing to recruit, hire and train armies of low-level employees.
‍
## II. Understanding AI Phone Agents in Call Centers[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#ii-understanding-ai-phone-agents-in-call-centers)
* Definition and basic capabilities
* Key features (e.g., natural language processing, 24/7 availability)
* Comparison to traditional automated systems
‍
AI Phone agents are not traditional automated prompt menus. We’ve all suffered through long options-packed menus read to us by a generic electronic voice.
‍
AI agents sound like people. They ask questions on their own and actually **understand** the responses of the person speaking to them. A chat with a well built AI agent should be indistinguishable (or better!) than one with a standard service representative.
‍
## III. Current Challenges in Call Center Operations[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#iii-current-challenges-in-call-center-operations)
### Tighter Margins[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#tighter-margins)
The landscape for call center operators is full of challenges. As network connectivity has improved worldwide, the ability to source operators has become a global market. And with an increased talent pool comes increased competition. Many “call centers” are operating virtually without the need for centralized equipment and connectivity.
‍
### Turnover and Training[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#turnover-and-training)
The biggest costs to call centers is maintaining quality across all of their operators. Call centers worldwide have notoriously high turnover rates with their employees and constantly struggle to find and retain good talent. As most call centers focus on entry-level employees, turnover due to upward mobility is also a significant factor. When employees walk out the door for other opportunities, they take their subject matter knowledge, and valuable on the job training expenses with them.
‍
### Inconsistent Customer Experiences[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#inconsistent-customer-experiences)
Beyond meeting the demand of customer call volumes centers are faced with the task of unifying customer experience across all of their representatives. This is where meticulous training and recording/quality assurance of calls comes into play. Maintaining an acceptable standard of customer experience proves to be an ever-present challenge. Few call centers can boast exceptional satisfaction rates.
### Limited Multi-Lingual Support[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#limited-multi-lingual-support)
Native english speakers come at a premium in the support call realm. Beyond that, bi-lingual speakers fetch even higher prices for call operator positions.
‍
Many call centers located outside of North America and Europe struggle with maintaining a high level of english (and other languages) comprehension across all representatives.
‍
## IV. How AI Phone Agents Address Call Center Challenges[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#iv-how-ai-phone-agents-address-call-center-challenges)
‍
AI phone agent teams can address the majority of challenges call centers are facing today.
### A. Cost reduction[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#a-cost-reduction)
‍
Agents enable you to scale the volume of calls your center handles without adding headcount. A common use case is maintaining more senior and experienced human operators while replacing entry level and tier 1 support staff with AI agents.
‍
### B. Improved consistency and quality[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#b-improved-consistency-and-quality)
‍
Following the scripts provided to employees can often be a challenges are caller requests vary, or simply from lack of proper training. AI agents share identical scripts, conversation flows, and knowledge bases of product/company information. This allows managers to make changes to a script or flow in a single place and instantly make that information known to all AI agents answering calls.
‍
With a centralized repository for directing your AI agents, call consistency can be guaranteed across all callers.
‍
### C. Scalability and flexibility[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#c-scalability-and-flexibility)
Capacity management is another area AI phone agents far exceed their human counterparts in call center activities. Peak caller times are often unexpected and can degrade a customer’s experience beyond repair if forced to wait for a human agent.
‍
AI agents are infinitely available, and can be built to handle spikes in call volumes with ease. Eliminating wait times and getting standardized call support to all of your customers.
‍
### D. Enhanced customer experience[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#d-enhanced-customer-experience)
Beyond their capacity to handle peak times, AI agents are available 24x7. Always standing by for calls that can be held in multiple languages. In an industry where bilingual employees are often essential, AI phone agents can seamlessly communicate in most languages.
‍
### E. Data collection and analytics[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#e-data-collection-and-analytics)
Bland has a powerful platform built around deriving insights from your agent’s calls. Our models can analyze the sentiment of your calls and help provide indicators that can be used for quality assurance modeling.
‍
Quality can be incredibly challenging to maintain across a large volume of calls happening around the clock. Bland insights allow you build customized insight reporting that automatically apply to each call as it’s happening. This means that insights steam directly to operators, giving them access to the pulse of their calls and how they are going.
‍
## V. Implementing AI Phone Agents in Call Centers[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#v-implementing-ai-phone-agents-in-call-centers)
‍
While all AI phone agent rollouts are unique to the company implementing them, almost all follow the same general framework to ensure success. The following are the steps that Bland engineers take whenever walking customers through a call center implementation.
‍
### Assessment of Current Operations[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#assessment-of-current-operations)
Calls can’t be improved if there are no insights into how they are going now. What are the scripts being used? How much variation typically occurs? What are the biggest challenges for your operators to understand and perform on any given call? The deeper these questions are answered in the early stage, the easier implementation and feedback collection will be further into the rollout.
‍
### Choosing the Right AI Solution[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#choosing-the-right-ai-solution)
AI is now a buzzword, we get it. So amidst the sea ‘AI tools’ how do you know what will actually work for your calls? Not all AI phone agents are created equal, and it’s not easy to differentiate what will work best. Again, this is where seasoned Engineers like Bland’s come into the picture. After assessing your calls and workflows, we can provide recommendations as to which strategy will best fit your call needs.
‍
### Integration with Existing Systems[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#integration-with-existing-systems)
An elegant integration must now be designed. The goal of this phase is to figure out how to hook new AI agents into your existing call workflows without a complete switchover. We want to divert a small trickle to AI operators before building a dam and redirecting all of the call volume.
‍
As every call center uses different technologies, this step is often very unique and customized to your business.
‍
### Training and Fine Tuning the AI[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#training-and-fine-tuning-the-ai)
Much like how you’d monitor a new call operator and provide feedback on their first few weeks of calls, the AI operators need a similar set of attention. Don’t despair, once this process occurs the models will remember their feedback **forever.**
‍
Depending on your use case, this stage is completed in collaboration with engineers who have spent years tweaking and optimizing call flows for customers.
‍
### Gradual Rollout and Evaluation[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#gradual-rollout-and-evaluation)
Once trained and fine-tuned models are performing well in their test phases, it’s time to get them onto real-world calls and monitor closely. Remember those monitoring and insights tools mentioned earlier? This is where your plan for evaluation comes into play. Monitor call transcripts, and all of your analysis factors in real time while your AI agents take those first few calls.
‍
In this stage, some undiscovered improvements often lead to minor adjustments to the agents. As your metrics and call satisfaction continue to improve, you will continue to direct more call volume to your newly trained agents.
‍
## VII. Challenges and Considerations[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#vii-challenges-and-considerations)
With any new technology costs of implementation need to be considered when evaluating if AI agents are right for your call center’s business model. In enterprise software, costs can come in far more packages than simple licensing fees. Here are our top challenges and costs to consider when evaluating an AI agent based solution for your call center.
‍
### Initial Investment and ROI[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#initial-investment-and-roi)
Much like hiring new employees, building fully automated AI systems and training them well takes some time and careful planning. It’s important to budget time for learning alongside your implementing engineers at Bland (or elsewhere), and to be prepared for feedback loops during training.
‍
While the costs of the technology or of making AI phone agent calls are not high, your time spent on the initial implementation may be significant.
‍
### Employee Concerns[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#employee-concerns)
AI has made headlines over the past few years as the killer of jobs, and for many entry level data-based positions this may actually be true. Call center organizations rely heavily on well trained staff, and there may be increased tensions if management is seen as trying to “replace” everyone with machines.
‍
### Data Privacy and Security[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#data-privacy-and-security)
Is sensitive data passed to your call operators? Does your specific industry require a unique treatment of user data? All data privacy and security questions matter greatly when architecting an AI solution. Bland works with companies from healthcare to fintech and can tailor security needs for everyone.
‍
### Maintaining a Human Element[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#maintaining-a-human-element)
At Bland we rarely recommend a fully automated call center solution. In most of our use cases, we use AI agents to handle a bulk of calls, while strategically passing some callers to highly trained human operators. Striking the right balance between automation and human interaction can often be a challenge and is worth thinking through before beginning any AI agent based project.
‍
## VIII. Future Trends in AI Call Center Technology[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#viii-future-trends-in-ai-call-center-technology)
‍
You’ve now read about what is possible with AI phone agents in call centers, and gained an understanding of how to see through your own integration projects. But what does the future hold for call center AI? At Bland we are excited (and already working on) several areas that will change call center operations forever.
‍
### Advanced Sentiment Analysis[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#advanced-sentiment-analysis)
This is something that is constantly improving at Bland, to answer the question “How are our calls going?”. As the sophistication of our large language models increases, so does our ability to understand the complexities of caller emotions during a call. Are they delighted with the support they’re receiving, flustered, angry? It can all be deduced by their speech.
‍
### Predictive Customer Service[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#predictive-customer-service)
One of hte most frustrating experiences with call customer service is having to explain the entirety of your situation to an agent (or multiple agents). Then you “wait while they pull up your account”, and still have to re-explain your question. With AI agents and advaced CRMs, all of this contextual information can be made available to the agent instantly. They would have immediate knowledge of all previous issues, current products etc.
‍
### Continuous Learning and Improvement[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#continuous-learning-and-improvement)
The best employees (both human and machine) learn from their mistakes and get better at their jobs over time. It’s why industry experience is often such a great indicator of abilities. As AI agents (and the systems teams like Bland build around them) grow in sophistication, there will come a time in the no-so-far future where the agents can be designed to “self learn” from their calls. While the Bland team has already figured this out, such a hands-off approach is not quite available to all users out of the box.
‍
## IX. Conclusion[#](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ai-phone-agents-revolutionizing-call-center-technology-and-profitability#ix-conclusion)
‍
Are AI phone agents the answer to you call center’s quality and profitability concerns? As you read today, the answer is very likely yes. But no technical solution is without potential drawbacks and costs. Before considering a major implementation of AI agents into your business, we strongly urge you take advantage of a consultative call with an experienced Engineer.
‍
At Bland, we have a team standing by to answer your questions and review your specific business use cases. Don’t hesitate to reach out and book a call, even if you’re not 100% certain of how a solution would work for your call center.
